The earthquake occurred at a depth of 173 kilometres.
The most recent earthquake to strike Nepal was on September 8.
The earthquake came amid ongoing rescue and recovery operations following floods triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26.
The disaster swept away homes, roads and bridges, damaged hydropower projects and left thousands missing.
Authorities have also raised concerns over the region’s vulnerability to extreme weather, glacier retreat and rising temperatures.
Chinese researchers have warned that climate change is accelerating glacier loss across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, potentially increasing the risks of future disasters.
The plateau is also the source of several major transboundary rivers, including the Brahmaputra, making environmental changes there a concern for downstream communities.

stories.headline: HP High Court Refuses To Reject Suit Challenging Cooperative Society Election, Says Defence Cannot Be Considered Under Order VII Rule 11 CPC
stories.title: HP High Court Refuses To Reject Suit Challenging Cooperative Society Election, Says Defence Cannot Be Considered Under Order VII Rule 11 CPC
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Himachal Pradesh High Court has reiterated that while deciding an application for rejection of a plaint under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, courts must confine their examination to the averments in the plaint and the documents accompanying it, without considering the defence raised by the defendants.

Dismissing a petition challenging the rejection of such an application in a dispute overthe election of a cooperative society's managing committee, the Court held that the trial court had rightly refused to reject the plaint at this stage.
The case arose from a dispute over the August 25, 2023 election of the managing committee of the Katohar Khurd Cooperative Agriculture Service Society in Una, Himachal Pradesh.
The plaintiffs alleged that their nomination forms had been illegally rejected and that the election process was conducted in violation of the prescribed rules.
They sought to declare the election null and void and requested the appointment of an administrator until fresh elections were held.
The defendants sought rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 CPC, arguing that the suit was barred under Sections 72 and 76 of the Himachal Pradesh Cooperative Societies Act, 1968.
After the trial court dismissed their application, the defendants approached the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution.
The High Court observed that an application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC must be decided solely on the basis of the plaint and accompanying documents, without considering the defendants' defence.

It held that the plaintiffs' contention regarding the delay in adjudication of the election dispute under Section 72 of the Himachal Pradesh Cooperative Societies Act, 1968, had been rightly considered by the trial court.
The Court further noted that a plaint cannot be partially rejected when multiple reliefs are sought and the suit cannot be rejected in its entirety.

Finding no grounds to interfere with the trial court's order under Article 227 of the Constitution, the High Court dismissed the petition, clarifying that its observations would not affect the merits of the underlying suit.

stories.headline: When households became shareholders: The quiet story of India's balance sheet
stories.title: When households became shareholders: The quiet story of India's balance sheet
stories.summary: On October 7, Prime Minister Narendra Modi completes 25 years in elected executive office: Nearly 13 as chief minister of Gujarat and more than 12 as prime minister. Assessments of that span usually tend to focus on politics or on governance. The quieter story is in India’s financial balance sheet and in the economic growth under his leadership. Individual investors now hold close to a fifth of listed Indian equities, directly or through mutual funds. That is roughly double their share since March 2014. Every month, Indian households put more than ₹32,000 crore into mutual funds through systematic investment plans.The Gujarat TemplateWhen Modi took charge in Gujarat in October 2001, the state was still reeling from the Kutch earthquake that January. He did not inherit a growth story; he had to build one. Gujarat had real advantages: A centuries-old trading culture, a long coastline with ports, strength in petrochemicals and textiles, and a cooperative tradition exemplified by Amul. What it needed was scale and execution.The priorities were practical. Dedicated feeders gave farms and villages reliable electricity. Roads, ports and industrial clusters followed, and check dams supported agriculture. The Vibrant Gujarat summits gave global investors direct access to the state government. The administration learnt to see projects through to completion. Today, Kutch, once written off, is one of India’s leading tourist destinations.That combination of infrastructure first, direct investor engagement and follow-through became the template later scaled nationally.Also Read: Built for Bharat: How India’s rails changed commerceFrom Ports to a Financial CentreThe clearest link between the Gujarat years and India’s financial present is GIFT City. It began as a state project and became India’s first International Financial Services Centre (IFSC). The ambition was explicit: To build in India what Singapore, Dubai and Hong Kong had built, an offshore-grade financial hub within our borders.The results are measurable. GIFT Connect—the link between the Singapore Exchange and NSE International Exchange (NSE IX)—was piloted in July 2022 and became fully operational in July 2023. It moved trading in India-linked derivatives from Singapore to GIFT City, bringing price discovery for a key Indian benchmark onshore.NSE IX has recorded average daily volumes above $5 billion in recent months, with open interest in the $20-25 billion range. Around $70-80 billion of bonds by Indian issuers have been listed on the exchange. It has also drawn foreign participants, including Sri Lankan bank bonds and a partnership with the Cyprus Stock Exchange.A region known for factories and ports is now building institutions that manage global capital.Formalising the EconomyIndia’s economy has roughly doubled in dollar terms since 2014, from about $2 trillion to little more than $4 trillion in 2026. The more consequential change has been in the economy’s structure.The Goods & Services Tax replaced a patchwork of central and state levies with a single national system. Its early rollout was bumpy, with compliance burdens and rate complexity that later reforms have tried to simplify. But it created a common market and a digital trail of transactions.The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code changed the balance between lenders and defaulters. Promoters could no longer assume a failing company would remain theirs indefinitely. E-invoicing and online filing drew more firms into the formal economy. This matters for capital markets. A company on the books builds a credit history, which opens the door to bank finance.The 2019 corporate tax cut, production-linked incentive schemes, and a sharp rise in public infrastructure spending aimed to make India a more competitive place to build and invest, providing strong policy impetus under Modi.From Inclusion to ParticipationCapital-market participation rests on basic financial access, and that access was built first. The Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–mobile framework brought hundreds of millions of Indians into the banking system. UPI made digital payments routine, even for a street vendor.In 2014, about 1.65 crore unique investors were registered with the NSE. Today there are more than 13.5 crore. Mutual fund assets have grown from around ₹8.25 lakh crore to about ₹87 lakh crore at present.Households Now Own India IncFor generations, Indian families kept their wealth in gold, land and fixed deposits, and equity markets belonged to traders and the wealthy. That is changing. With individuals now holding close to 20 percent of listed equities through direct and indirect channels, a larger share of corporate India’s profits flows back to ordinary savers.New Channels for CapitalToday, when it comes to capital markets, companies have access to a wider range of funding than bank loans alone.Newer channels are opening too: Since 2018, 14 municipal corporations—five of them in Gujarat—have raised about ₹2,565 crore through 18 bond issues on the NSE, while more than 750 small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are now listed on NSE Emerge, a dedicated platform for SMEs. The Social Stock Exchange, meanwhile, has drawn in over 200 registered non-profits, 16 of whose projects have together raised ₹44.5 crore from investors.Over 25 years, the public service arc for Modi runs from rebuilding an earthquake-struck state to building an international financial centre. Modi’s stated philosophy is Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas, Sabka Prayas: Together with all, development for all, the trust of all, the effort of all. In capital markets, at least, that phrase has taken a concrete form: The growth of Indian enterprise is increasingly being funded by Indian savers.

opening: On October 7, Prime Minister Narendra Modi completes 25 years in elected executive office: Nearly 13 as chief minister of Gujarat and more than 12 as prime minister.
Assessments of that span usually tend to focus on politics or on governance.
body: The quieter story is in India’s financial balance sheet and in the economic growth under his leadership.
Individual investors now hold close to a fifth of listed Indian equities, directly or through mutual funds.
That is roughly double their share since March 2014.
Every month, Indian households put more than ₹32,000 crore into mutual funds through systematic investment plans.
The Gujarat Template.
When Modi took charge in Gujarat in October 2001, the state was still reeling from the Kutch earthquake that January.
He did not inherit a growth story; he had to build one.
Gujarat had real advantages: A centuries-old trading culture, a long coastline with ports, strength in petrochemicals and textiles, and a cooperative tradition exemplified by Amul.
What it needed was scale and execution.
The priorities were practical.
Dedicated feeders gave farms and villages reliable electricity.
Roads, ports and industrial clusters followed, and check dams supported agriculture.
The Vibrant Gujarat summits gave global investors direct access to the state government.
The administration learnt to see projects through to completion.
Today, Kutch, once written off, is one of India’s leading tourist destinations.
That combination of infrastructure first, direct investor engagement and follow-through became the template later scaled nationally.
From Ports to a Financial Centre.
The clearest link between the Gujarat years and India’s financial present is GIFT City.
It began as a state project and became India’s first International Financial Services Centre (IFSC).
The ambition was explicit: To build in India what Singapore, Dubai and Hong Kong had built, an offshore-grade financial hub within our borders.
The results are measurable.
GIFT Connect—the link between the Singapore Exchange and NSE International Exchange (NSE IX)—was piloted in July 2022 and became fully operational in July 2023.
It moved trading in India-linked derivatives from Singapore to GIFT City, bringing price discovery for a key Indian benchmark onshore.
NSE IX has recorded average daily volumes above $5 billion in recent months, with open interest in the $20-25 billion range.
Around $70-80 billion of bonds by Indian issuers have been listed on the exchange.
It has also drawn foreign participants, including Sri Lankan bank bonds and a partnership with the Cyprus Stock Exchange.
A region known for factories and ports is now building institutions that manage global capital.
Formalising the Economy.
India’s economy has roughly doubled in dollar terms since 2014, from about $2 trillion to little more than $4 trillion in 2026.
The more consequential change has been in the economy’s structure.
The Goods & Services Tax replaced a patchwork of central and state levies with a single national system.
Its early rollout was bumpy, with compliance burdens and rate complexity that later reforms have tried to simplify.
But it created a common market and a digital trail of transactions.
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code changed the balance between lenders and defaulters.
Promoters could no longer assume a failing company would remain theirs indefinitely.
E-invoicing and online filing drew more firms into the formal economy.
This matters for capital markets.
A company on the books builds a credit history, which opens the door to bank finance.

The 2019 corporate tax cut, production-linked incentive schemes, and a sharp rise in public infrastructure spending aimed to make India a more competitive place to build and invest, providing strong policy impetus under Modi.
From Inclusion to ParticipationCapital-market participation rests on basic financial access, and that access was built first.
The Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–mobile framework brought hundreds of millions of Indians into the banking system.
UPI made digital payments routine, even for a street vendor.
In 2014, about 1.65 crore unique investors were registered with the NSE.
Today there are more than 13.5 crore.
Mutual fund assets have grown from around ₹8.25 lakh crore to about ₹87 lakh crore at present.
Households.
Now Own India IncFor generations, Indian families kept their wealth in gold, land and fixed deposits, and equity markets belonged to traders and the wealthy.
That is changing.
With individuals now holding close to 20 percent of listed equities through direct and indirect channels, a larger share of corporate India’s profits flows back to ordinary savers.
New Channels for CapitalToday, when it comes to capital markets, companies have access to a wider range of funding than bank loans alone.

Newer channels are opening too: Since 2018, 14 municipal corporations—five of them in Gujarat—have raised about ₹2,565 crore through 18 bond issues on the NSE, while more than 750 small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are now listed on NSE Emerge, a dedicated platform for SMEs.
The Social Stock Exchange, meanwhile, has drawn in over 200 registered non-profits, 16 of whose projects have together raised ₹44.5 crore from investors.
Over 25 years, the public service arc for Modi runs from rebuilding an earthquake-struck state to building an international financial centre.
Modi’s stated philosophy is Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas, Sabka Prayas: Together with all, development for all, the trust of all, the effort of all.
In capital markets, at least, that phrase has taken a concrete form: The growth of Indian enterprise is increasingly being funded by Indian savers.

stories.headline: India will support every meaningful effort to bring peace to Ukraine, West Asia: PM Modi
stories.title: India will support every meaningful effort to bring peace to Ukraine, West Asia: PM Modi
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 22: India and Poland on Thursday agreed to deepen ties in defence, space, and nuclear energy domains, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Polish counterpart Donald Tusk pledging to boost bilateral strategic partnership amid growing global instability. Following the talks, Modi said both sides believe in democratic values and the rule of law and that India will continue to support every meaningful effort in bringing peace to Ukraine and West Asia. Tusk is on a three-day visit to India amid renewed global push to end the conflict in Ukraine. "Today we have agreed to deepen ties in defence, space, and nuclear energy. We invite Polish companies to engage in co-development and co-production with India in all these strategic areas," Modi said. "In critical minerals and coal gasification too, we will develop new partnerships with Polish expertise," he added. Modi said the friendship between India and Poland is based not only on diplomatic relations but also on a shared heritage of humanity and compassion. "During World War II, the royal families of Jamnagar and Kolhapur sheltered thousands of Polish children and families in India." "Poland also extended this spirit of humanity by supporting the safe return of our students from Ukraine in 2022," he added. In his media statement, Modi also made a mention of the growing economic engagement between the two countries. "The world is going through a period of uncertainty and change. Even at this time, both India and Poland are emerging as important centres of growth, technology, and innovation," he said. The prime minister said the growing economic strength of the two countries has created new opportunities for India-Poland partnership. "And the India-European Union free trade agreement has further expanded these opportunities. Upon entry into force, this agreement will open up new opportunities for exports of machinery, chemicals, plastics, and engineering goods from India to Poland," he said. "Additionally, we will attract new investments from Poland in sectors such as railways and mobility, advanced manufacturing, food processing, and biotech," he said. Modi also exuded confidence that India and Poland will work together to develop trusted supply chains for the world, and also realise the shared goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030.

stories.headline: Iran’s IRGC says 4 ships hit, set ablaze in Gulf; 3 others strike mines near Hormuz
stories.title: Iran’s IRGC says 4 ships hit, set ablaze in Gulf; 3 others strike mines near Hormuz
stories.summary: Tehran , October 22: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has claimed that it struck and set fire to four ships carrying oil cargoes in the northern Persian Gulf, while three other vessels collided with mines in the western Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian state media, Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB). In a statement issued on Thursday, the IRGC Navy said the four ships had previously crossed an “illegal route” despite warnings to the maritime companies operating them. “Following previous warnings to the offending maritime companies, who had been deceived by the invading US military and had crossed illegal routes, Navy fighters, by observing and pursuing four offending ships, which had previously crossed the illegal route, discovered them transferring oil cargoes in the middle of the northern Persian Gulf, where all four ships were hit simultaneously and caught fire,” the statement said, as reported by IRIB. The IRGC Navy also claimed that three other vessels had struck mines in the western Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday night and were stopped. The statement came amid heightened tensions over maritime movement through the strategically important waterway, through which a significant share of global oil shipments passes. Reiterating its control over the strait, the IRGC Navy said its personnel continued to manage maritime movement with the support of the Iranian public. “With this enormous national support, the IRGC Navy sailors continue to manage and control the Strait of Hormuz,” the statement said. The Iranian force also blamed the United States for the reported maritime incidents, accusing Washington of encouraging vessels to navigate through "illegally mined passage". "The insistence of the arrogant US regime on inciting ships to pass through the illegally mined passage has increased maritime incidents day by day," the statement said. Issuing a warning to Washington, the IRGC Navy said the confrontation could expand if the situation continued. "The aggressive US army should know that if this trend continues, the scope of the confrontation will be extended to the aggressive bases in the region. This is a serious warning," it added. The statement did not identify the vessels involved or provide details about their ownership, the extent of the reported damage or any casualties. The claim of strikes on the ships came as US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) said that the United States is not negotiating with Iran and "something" will happen "fairly soon." Speaking to American news network NewsNation 's White House correspondent Libbey Dean, Trump was asked about developments in negotiations with Tehran; Trump initially acknowledged some activity but indicated that the outcome remained uncertain. “A little bit, but we'll see what happens,” Trump said when asked whether negotiations with Iran were ongoing. Asked whether he was done negotiating with the Iranian government, Trump said, "No, I think we're not negotiating...we are going to have something, one way or the other. It'll happen fairly soon." In the interview, Trump also highlighted the situation between Washington and Tehran as "a little conflict against Iran" and said the United States was performing well on both military and economic fronts. "I think our sanctions ended the real deal over there. But we're doing very well militarily and financially against Iran," he said. Trump did not specify what action or development he expected to take place “fairly soon” or provide a definitive timeline for the next steps in the US approach towards Iran. All the developments come amid the report by The New York Times that the United States and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after the American midterm elections, while Tehran has threatened to unveil a weapon it calls the "father of all bombs" amid escalating tensions in West Asia. According to The New York Times, the US and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for a short but intensive operation targeting Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. Citing US officials and other people briefed on the deliberations, the report said the two militaries have stepped up exercises, including flying aircraft over Iraq to practise strike manoeuvres. Amid the possibility of renewed strikes, Iran has warned that it would respond to any renewed military action. According to Iranian state-affiliated media outlet Student News Network (SNN), IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said, "The United States has the ‘Mother of All Bombs.’ We will show them the ‘Father of All Bombs,’ and it will definitely be something new for them." But Tehran has not provided details about the weapon or clarified what the threat entails. The warning follows reports that US President Donald Trump has considered using the 22,000-pound GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), known as the "Mother of All Bombs", against Iran’s deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility. According to The New York Times, the United States is assembling a substantial military force expected to be fully in place by early November, including three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces. Officials have cited political considerations, including Trump’s earlier pledge not to strike Iran before the midterm elections, as reasons the operation could be delayed. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, meanwhile, has highlighted the situation as a major challenge for Tehran. In an address to the Iranian Parliament, Pezeshkian said, "The memorandum of understanding we signed was very good; we hadn't given anything. The current situation is neither good for us, nor for the region, nor for the world." He added, "We are in a super-challenge, not a challenge. America didn't think we would stand firm despite the pressure and war, but we stood firm, and we will continue to stand firm." The New York Times report said Washington was seeking to use the prospect of renewed military action as leverage in negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme and control over the Strait of Hormuz. However, Iranian negotiators have resisted making concessions on the nuclear issue, insisting that the matter be deferred until later in the talks. As military preparations and diplomatic efforts continue, the possibility of renewed strikes has raised concerns about a wider regional conflict, with uncertainty persisting over Trump’s final decision and Iran’s potential response. (ANI)

America didn't think we would stand firm despite the pressure and war, but we stood firm, and we will continue to stand firm." The New York Times report said Washington was seeking to use the prospect of renewed military action as leverage in negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme and control over the Strait of Hormuz.
However, Iranian negotiators have resisted making concessions on the nuclear issue, insisting that the matter be deferred until later in the talks.

As military preparations and diplomatic efforts continue, the possibility of renewed strikes has raised concerns about a wider regional conflict, with uncertainty persisting over Trump’s final decision and Iran’s potential response.

The warning follows reports that US President Donald Trump has considered using the 22,000-pound GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), known as the "Mother of All Bombs", against Iran’s deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility.

The IRGC Navy also claimed that three other vessels had struck mines in the western Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday night and were stopped.

stories.headline: Delhi High Court Reserves Verdict On Neha Bora's Plea Against Peace Bond Notice Amid Anti-CEC Protests, Judgment Tomorrow
stories.title: Delhi High Court Reserves Verdict On Neha Bora's Plea Against Peace Bond Notice Amid Anti-CEC Protests, Judgment Tomorrow
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Delhi High Court on Thursday (October 22) reserved its verdict on a plea by National President of All India Students Association (AISA) Neha Bora challenging a notice to execute a personal bond of ₹10,000 with one surety to maintain peace during an inquiry, following her participation in 'Lehra Do Tiranga' protest on October 16.
After hearing the parties for over 2.5 hours, Justice Subramonium Prasad reserved its verdict and said that orders will be pronounced on Friday at 6pm.

Bora has challenged an October 17 notice issued by a Special Executive Magistrate under Sections 126 (Magistrate may show cause an individual why peace bond may not be executed if he receives information that a person is likely commit a breach of the peace) and 130(when the Magistrate acting under section 126, section 127, section 128 or section 129, deems it necessary to require any person to show cause under he shall make an order in writing mentioning certain particulars) BNSS, read with Section 135(3) BNSS.

Under Section 135(3) Magistrate can, for reasons to be recorded in writing, direct the person in respect of whom the order under section 130 has been made to execute a bond or bail bond, for keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour until the conclusion of the inquiry and may detain him in custody until such bond or bail bond is executed or, in default of execution, until the inquiry is concluded.

The proviso states where no proceedings are taken against a person under sections 127, 128, or 129 then such person shall not be directed to execute a bond or bail bond for maintaining good behaviour.
Section 135(1) empowers magistrate to inquire into the truth of the information upon which action has been taken against a person who appears, based on show cause notice under Section 130.

Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan appearing for Bora said that the petitioner, a leader of AISA, had made a protest call on October 16 which was peaceful and she had never called for any violence.
He said that when Bora went to Mandi house on the evening of October 16, she was detained 10-15 mins later.
On that date she has not guilty of any offence, including that of breaching peace, he said.

He said that Bora's detention was completely illegal and that she was not involved in a separate protest call given by another organization, i.e., CJP protest to unfurl National Flag at Connaught Place Central Park.
He said that after Bora was detained she was not allowed to reach out immediately to her family or lawyers.

He said that Section 163 BNSS (Power of Executive Magistrate to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger) was not invoked in the area from where Bora was detained, however loudspeakers on the location announced that Section 163 was applicable.

stories.headline: Telangana allows in-principle sanctions for urban projects under Centre’s Urban Challenge Fund
stories.title: Telangana allows in-principle sanctions for urban projects under Centre’s Urban Challenge Fund
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Telangana government has authorised the State Mission Director of the Urban Challenge Fund (UCF) to grant in-principle administrative sanctions for projects proposed by urban local bodies, subject to specified approvals.

An order issued by the Municipal Administration Department on October 22 directs urban local bodies across the State to follow the operational guidelines issued by the Union Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs for the Urban Challenge Fund and its Credit Repayment Guarantee Sub-scheme (CRGSS), and to submit proposals accordingly.

The in-principle sanctions can be granted for projects approved by the State Level High Powered Committee and forwarded to the Centre for approval, provided their Preliminary Project Reports have also been cleared by the Finance Department.
The Mission Director may stipulate additional conditions for individual projects while granting sanctions to enable preparatory works to begin.
The Commissioner and Director of Municipal Administration has been directed to take further action for submitting proposals for administrative sanction under the two schemes.

The government had earlier designated the Secretary of the Municipal Administration Department as the State Mission Director and constituted State-level technical and high-powered committees to scrutinise and approve projects under the fund.

The Urban Challenge Fund (UCF) is a centrally sponsored scheme of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) with a central assistance of ₹1,00,000 crore for the five year period ending 2030–31.
It seeks to shift India’s urban policy from grant-based funding to market-linked development, with emphasis on private investment.

The scheme envisages projects with a minimum 50% funding through market linked sources such as banks, municipal bonds and private funding, and 25% each from the Central and State governments based on the fulfilment of the condition.
